RAJYA SABHA 
Thursday, the 24th March, 2005/3 Chaitra, 1926 (Saka)] 
 The House met at eleven of the clock, 
MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair.  
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Blue Print of Tsunami Warning System 
*321.     SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR:†† 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Canadian scientist accompanying the Canadian Prime Minister 
during his recent New Delhi visit, made presentation of a blue print for setting 
up a Tsunami Warning Centre in the Indian Ocean; 
(b) if so, the broad features and estimated cost of the Tsunami Warning Centre 
and whether the system is proposed to be set up in a joint venture between the 
Ocean States; 
(c) whether the scientist had made such an offer before Tsunami disaster also; 
and 
(d) if so, Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a ) Yes, Sir. Dr. Tad Murthy, a 
Canadian expert, made a presentation on various aspects of Tsunami 
generation, propogation, preparedness a nd mitigation in general, during the 
Brain Storming Session entitled 'Great Tsunami Event of 26 December 2004' held 
on 21-22 January 2005 in New Delhi. 
(b) The Government is setting up a Tsunami and Storm Surges Warning System 
at an estimated cost of Rs. 125 crores with the following components: 
* Strengthening of the existing seismological network to indicate in near 
real time occurrence of a tsunamigenic earthquake. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati Sukhbuns Kaur. 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
* Installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean bottom at 
appropriate locales in the Indian Ocean, with real time connectivity. 
* Tide gauge and data buoys networking. 
* Modelling of the inundation scenarios for the entire coast. 
* The establishment of a center for collection of the information, analysis and 
generating status advisories. 
No, Sir. The system is not proposed to be set up as a joint venture 
between India and other Indian Ocean States; 
(c) No Sir. 
(d) Does not arise. 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, December 26th tragedy left behind a 
trail of death and destruction killing thousands of people and leaving 
thousands homeless. Foremost among the issues thrown up by this tragedy was the 
need for Tsunami warning system and a good coastal management programme. The 
hon. Minister has stated that the Government is setting up a Tsunami and storm 
surges warning system at an estimated cost of Rs. 125 crores. Sir, I would like 
to know from the hon. Minister whether there is a possibility of bringing Sri 
Lanka, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia as also certain 
African countries along the rim of the Indian Ocean which (are as vulnerable, 
into the loop on cost and information sharing basis;and whether senior 
representatives of the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank met 
Government officials and whether setting up of Tsunami warning system was 
discussed; and is there a possibility of financial data? 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairrman, Sir, as far as collaborating with our 
neighbours is concerned which the hon. Member has asked, I just want to inform 
the hon. Member that this has been discussed at various international 
conferences and we have taken the position and rightly so, that the Tsunami 
system is going to be set up with us. But that does not mean that we are not 
going to collaborate with our neighbours. So, what we are going to do is that we 
will set up the system and then collaborate network with all our neighbours so 
that the information that we have is tran smitted in real time to them so that it 
helps both sides. As far as discussions with the World Bank and other 
organisations are concerned, 
2 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
no, there has been no discussion in the context of sharing or in the context of aid 
because we don't need aid. This will cost us Rs. 125 crores and it is well within 
our reach an we can do it ourselves. 
SHRIMAT ISUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, we seem to be putting all our disaster 
mitigation eggs in the "Reactive Basket" of Rescue, Recovery, Relief, 
Rehabilitation, Reconstruction, Repair, Renewal and Retrofitting. None of the 
1000 plus cities along India's 6000 km coastal stretch has even one line of 
either cyclone or sea erosion protection, despite all being incorporated in the 
operative bye-laws and development control rules. Despite Coastal Zoning 
Regulation no audit or enforcement has taken place. I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister whether any steps have taken place for good coastal 
management, which I think, would have three components-regulation, education 
and social mobilization. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: As far as coastal management is concerned, Sir, this is 
not really within the purview of the Ministry of Science and Technology There is of 
course, a Central legislation to this effect and we hope that the State Governments 
which have coastal areas will effectively and strictly enforce the coastal 
regulations. The hon. Member is right that as we see on the ground today, the 
coastal regulations are not put into effect as quickly as it is required. So, I hope 
the State Government will take note of this and enforce them very strictly.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, there are two parts to this question. The first part 
relates to what Tad Murthy has said and the second part relates to what 
recommendations Dr. Swaminathan has made. As far as Dr.Swaminathan's 
recommendations are concerned, Sir, they are in the context of the fact that along 
the coasts, nature provides us with protection; and when nature provides us with 
protection, this is in the form of mangroves, this is in the form of coral reefs, 
this is in the form of sand 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
embankments. Now, when man destroys those protections, then, we cannot be protected 
from nature. So, what Dr. Swaminathan has said that 'yes; we must ensure that human beings 
don't destroy those mangroves'. And, now, this is up to the civil society, this is up to the State 
Governments, this is up to all the States who are along the coasts to ensure that the 
mangroves are not destroyed. As far as we are concerned, those that have been destroyed, the 
Central Government and my Ministry are working along with Dr. Swaminathan to, in fact, 
regenerate the mangroves to ensure that those are protected. 
As far ad Tad Mutiny is concerned, Sir, I might say that we have, in India, the 
expertise available to set up the Tsunami system ourselves. We have both the scientific 
talent as well as the resources, and the I dare say that what we have, other countries, 
including the Pacific countries, don't have. In a recent Conference held in Paris where 
the Secretary of the Ministry was the leader, the Pacific countries realised that what we 
are talking about is a system which is far superior to the system, at the moment, prevalent 
in the Pacific countries. So, we have the capability and we are setting it up. 
 
Įी कलराज िमĮ:तो उसके िलए क्या कोई कॉÛसेÛट्रेट करने की कोिशश की गई 
है,लोगɉ को लाने के िलए? 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, we already have a project in place; we have the costing in 
place; we know the steps that we are going to take; we have experts in place; everything is 
moving along as we had envisaged. 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Sir, I have seen the reply given by the hon. 
Minister.There is no joint venture regarding the Tsunami disaster system. However, I would 
like to know from the Minister whether it is a fact that a bilateral cooperation between India 
and Canada is going to be envisaged in the fields of science and technology, environment, 
trade and industry. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, that has nothing to do with this question. 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Sir, India before the Tsunami struck on 26th of 
December did not share the information with some of the countries which have been the 
members of the Tsunami warning sharing system namely, Australia, the United States of 
America, etc. In this area, almost all the countries are members of that system. Japan has 
an expertise in 
4 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
this regard. Apart from Tsunami-warning system, they give training to the people 
to protect themselves from the Tsunami disasters. Deaths are much less in Japan. 
When a Tsunami takes place, the people are evacuated within no minute. So, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the Indian Government is 
going to join the Consortium. This is first part of my question. 
Sir, the second part of my question is, whether the Government is going to 
utilise the expertise of Japan for the purpose of protecting the people who are 
living in the coastal areas which are affected by it by giving training to the people 
of the various States, who are in the fields for the purpose of helping them. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, I would like to respond to hon. Member by 
saying that these are two separate issues altogether. Sir, as far as the Pacific 
countries are concerned, you might note that there is a continuing fault in the 
Pacific Ocean and along all the countries of the Pacific Ocean. And, eighty per 
cent of all seismic energy is released in the Pacific Ocean. That has nothing to do 
with the Indian Ocean. Even if we were to join the consortium of the Pacific 
Ocean, it will not give us any inform ation about the Tsunami in the Indian 
Ocean. What we are talking about is a system for a Tsunami warning in the 
Indian Ocean with respect to coastal areas within the Indian Ocean. Now, that 
has the Eastern Coast of India, Sir Lanka, Sumatra, Java, Myanmar, Africa, 
right up to South Africa. So, we have to set up a system of our own. The 
expertise and the information available in the Pacific warning system have no 
impact on us. Therefore, the question of our joining them doesn't arise. As far as 
the other expertise in Japan is concerned, I might just mention to my learned 
friend, the hon. Member, that sixty per cent of all warnings issued under the 
Japanese Tsunami Warning System have been false alarms. So, we want to set 
up an expertise far better than the Japanese system, which we are going to do. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Sir, through you, I would like to ask 
the hon. Minister whether he is aware that the School of Oceanographic Studies, 
Jadhavpur University, West Bengal, have commented long back, even in the mid-
1990s, in different newspapers, that the modelling of long wavelength basement 
undulation and geoid anomalies indicate buckling of the entire lithosphere in 
response to the North-South compression. They have also warned that evidences 
like intra-plate seismicity, earthquake 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
strain, energy release pattern, marine  geophysical seismic profiling and fault 
plane solution results, indicate that the intraplate region of the Bay of Bengal is 
subjected to a North-Sourth compassive deformation. If so, is the hon. Minister 
aware of this and is the Ministry contemplating to set up an institute to find out, 
particularly... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please, put your question. Mr. Manoj Bhattacharya, 
please put your question. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Sir, th at is my question. Is the hon. 
Minister contemplating setting up these sorts of institutes in the Jadhavpur 
University for further studies? Are they going to be augmented? From the 
research paper I find, and it is evident, that they had such an idea and they had 
given some warning. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That's right. That's right. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: I would like to know whether the 
Ministry is contemplating to strengthen the research activities in the 
Jadhavpur University, the School of Oceanography. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is enough. Please, take your seat. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, there are two aspects to this question. Here, we 
are discussing the tsunami warning system. The question does not relate to the 
tectonic activity that is taking place ...(Interruption)... between the Indian tectonic 
plate and the Burmese tectonic plate. My learned friend, the hon. Member, is talking 
about the friction that is being caused between these two plates. Not just the 
Jadhavpur University, but also the NGRI and several of our institutions, have 
gone in depth into the matter as far as tectonic activity is concerned. We 
measure the intensity of, what is called, the movement magnitude. This is exactly 
what we do and we have great expertise in it. But, if otherwise, my learned 
friend, the hon. Member, wants the resources of the Jadhavpur University to be 
augmented, there is no problem in discussing that issue. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Sir, this may sound strange, but there was a report 
in the papers recently that there could be tsunamis in the Himalayas, because with 
global warming, huge lakes can be formed. There was a report in the papers that 
if those lakes burst, there could be havoc in North India. I am aware that the hon. 
Minister is in-charge of the Department of Oceanography. But this is a 
question, either himself, or refer it to the 
6 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
concerned Ministry, because the possibility of a tsunami in the Himalayas, 
although it may sound very strange, is also now within the reach of global 
warming. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Sir, I thank the hon. Member for raising this issue. I 
can assure the hon. Member, not that I Know of it, but I shall certainly sit with 
my officers and find out the authenticity of it, the feasibility of it and what we 
can do about it. 
Creation of Special Economic Regions 
*322.     SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI:† 
             DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Planning Commission has pr oposed the creation of Special 
Economic Regions in the country; 
(b) if so, whether Planning Commission has sent a note to Ministry of 
Commerce to consider creation of five or six very large Special Economic 
Regions instead of the SEZs; 
(c) whether proposed Economic Regions would be set up with world-class 
infrastructure and would not be meant for experts only; 
(d) whether Government have considered the suggestions made by the 
Planning Commission; and 
(e) if so, by what time a final decision in this regard is likely to be 
taken? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. Planning Commission has not proposed the creation of Special 
Economic Regions (SER). SER is a concept suggested by a team of NRI 
professionals who made a presentation on "India FDI project", in December 2004. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the house by Shrimati Ambika 
Soni. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
The team in its presentation pointed out that there are too many SEZs. Only 
five to ten should be targeted, which would be large and preferably be called 
Special Economic Regions (SER). They should have world-class infrastructure 
including all the facilities of a township, such as an airport, educational 
institutions, etc., and should have a more flexible labour regime. -Particular emphasis 
was laid on Fast Track Courts in the SER, particularly for Intellectual Property 
Rights. 
(b) to (e) Does not arise. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, I have gone through the short reply 
given by the Government. But the question raised by me pertains to a 
discussion, which has been held in this country from the time when the 
present Prime Minister was the Finance Minister and even before that. 
The importance of Special Economic Zones has not ever been underplayed 
because of the goals set for FDI, it being such a competitive field for this entire 
region, the importance of it cannot be overemphasized. I just want to know one 
thing from the Government. This proposal was revived by the earlier 
Government in 2004 and, even if the Planning Commission has not yet sent 
their proposals to the Government, it is in the pipeline, as we are told and we 
understand. I would like to know, by when the Government would think of 
spelling out their policy on Special Economic Zones. We are losing out in this 
highly competitive market. Infrastructure takes a long time to be set in place. 
I would like to know what are the proposals in this regard. 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, at present, the con cept of Special 
Economic Region, as has been pointed out by the hon; Member herself, has not 
been mooted by the Planning Commission, nor is it the Government of India's 
proposal. The suggestion for setting up a Special Economic Region, as has 
been pointed out by the hon. Member, was by a group of foreign NRIs, and, at 
that time, at the presentation of "Indi a FDI Project" this suggestion was made. 
Sir, at present, there are a number of economic zones which have been operating in 
the country. Now, I would like to just point out the difference between the Special 
Economic Zone and the Special Economic Region. The Special Economic Zone is 
specifically delineated duty-free enclave deemed to be foreign territory for the 
purpose of trade 
8 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
operation, duties and tariffs. As far as Special Economic Region is concerned, 
high quality infrastructure is needed to achieve that degree of development, and 
Sir, this includes the improved infrastructure including the world-class airports, 
specialised communication system, reliable power, transport, internationally 
competitive business environment, etc.,etc. These are the things. As far as the 
Special Economic Zones are concerned, I would like to share with like to share 
with the House, through you, Sir, that the minimum size required is thousand 
acres. Then the primary focus is on export. Then, the status customs bonded. 
The Administration is with Development Commissioner. He is in-charge. These 
are the things, which are put as far as the Special Economic Zones are concerned. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: I am grateful for the information supplied. 
This information really pertains to my question. The question is that we learnt 
that this proposal of setting up 23 Special Economic zones have been 
entrusted to the Group of Ministers, but that apart NRIs proposal was for five 
or six regions which is quite different. I want to ask the Government that in 
the meantime — in all these delays, consideration and reconsideration, the 
Government of India and Group of Ministers looking into the proposal—the State 
Governments are setting up their own barriers, spelling out their own incentives. In 
the meantime, China has overtaken us by almost quarter of a century. We are 
already too late. I know the infrastructure requirement. But that infrastructure has 
to be put up at some time and within a time-frame. Otherwise, we are going to 
miss the bus. I want to know: why can't the Central Government announce a 
unified policy for the entire country instead of having State Governments set up 
their own barriers? 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, at present, each State, as pointed out by 
the hon. Member, has enacted legislation to create Special Economic Zones. Now, as 
far as the Central Legislation is concerned, it is before the Group of Ministers. As 
soon as the decision is taken, the House will be kept informed. 
DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, last year... (interruptions).. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Are you not satisfied with the answer? 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: He is repeating my question. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Are you repeating the same question? 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY: No, I am asking a different question. Last year, 
during the visit of hon. Prime Minister to the United States of America, a number of 
NRIs approached the hon. Prime Minister. They were asked by hon. Prime 
Minister for a roadmap, and asked as to how to make India an attractive place for 
FDI. Accordingly, a group of NRIs came to India. They pleaded with the 
Government. Since 23 Zones, which the previous Government set up, will not be 
practical, they advised to have six Special Economic Regions with all 
infrastructure. ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Don't make a speech. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: I would like to know what is the line of 
action because we heard that the Planning Commission is planning to give a 
suggestion to have six Special Economic Zones. What is the Government's 
stand? What can we expect? 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, I have already replied to that question. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Don't repeat your answer.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, recently in one of the speeches, it was 
said that the country would be divided into different economic zones in 
accordance with the natural advantages. If that is the case, in what way they are 
different from the Special Economic Zones, which the Minister has 
announced. 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, regarding advantages, as far as the 
Special Economic Zones are concerned,  there is 100 per cent tax exemption 
for the first five years, 50 per cent tax exemption for the next two years, and, 
then up to 50 per cent of the profits ploughed back for the next three years. Now, 
this is as it exists. 
As far as the encashment of income tax benefits is concerned, the proposal 
was for 100 per cent tax exemption for the first five years, 50 per cent for the next 
five years, and 50 per cent of the re-invested profit for the next 10 years, that is a 
total of 20 years. 
SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Sir, through you, I would like to say that Special 
Economic Zones is a good thing, but the problem is that we have far too many 
small economic zones in the country. What we need is a bigger one and the 
neighbouring States must cooperate. Otherwise, the infrastructure fails there, and, 
therefore, the economic zones are not progressing as much as they should. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: This is a good suggestion." Please keep it in mind. 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister: how many SEZs have been created so far, what is the experience so far, 
and, what are the applications that have come from different States and are still 
pending with the Government of India, and, also about the time-frame in this 
regard? 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, now there are already eight economic 
zones... (Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You have already replied ...(Interruptions)...

Visit of Afghan President to India 
*323.    PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:† 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Afghanistan President during his visit to India has impressed upon 
India that he would take up the issue about Indian goods being able to enter 
Afghanistan through Pakistan; 
(b) if so, whether the two agreements were signed between India and 
Afghanistan; 
(c) if so, to what extent these agreements would be helpful for both the 
countries; 
(d) whether Indian Airlines would begin flying the Delhi-Kabul sector from 
March 27; and 
(e) what are the other assistance that would be provided to Afghanistan by 
India during 2005-06? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (e) A Statement is placed on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Afghan Government has conveyed that transit access for Indian goods, 
and in particular for those under India's assistance programmes, would facilitate 
in strengthening Afghanistan's reconstruction effort. Afghan leaders have also 
indicated that they would pursue the issue of transit for Indian goods with the 
Government of Pakistan. 
(b) and (c) Two MOUs were signed during the visit of President Karzai. The 
MOU on Cooperation in the field of media and information calls for greater 
interaction between media persons and radio and TV organization of the two

Capability of ports for modern vessels 
*332. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Country's ports are capable of handling new generation 
vessels; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the steps taken by Government to make these ports capable of 
handling new generation vessels? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (c) Lack of globally comparable port 
infrastructure, mainly, inadequate depth in port channels and basins and cargo 
handling facilities which include berths, terminals, cargo handling equipments, 
etc. limit the capacity of Indian ports to handle new generation vessels. It is not, 
however, economically prudent to make investments in creating infrastructure for 
handling new generation vessels for all commodity categories in all the ports. 
Creation of infrastructure in the major ports depends on the present cargo mix 
in these ports, future traffic potential for various categories of cargo, assessment of 
the categories of vessels which may call at these ports, etc, after taking into 
account the demands of maritime trade. This is an on-going process. As part of 
this process, major ports undertake capital dredging for deepening of port basins and 
channels from time to time to keep pace with the draught requirements of 
vessels calling at these ports, construct new berths, expand existing berths and 
also acquire/upgrade their cargo handling equipment.

Review of IT Act, 2000 
2510. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) the terms of reference of the Expert Panel set up to review the 
Information Technology Act, 2000 and were the compulsion of Government to set 
up this Panel when the Act was promulgated only four years ago; 
(b) whether any structural deficiencies in  the Act or lack of foresight of 
variegated issues relating to e-governance and cyber laws, off shoring clients 
raising questions about India's data-protection laws, etc. at that point of time 
in 2000; and 
(c) whether Government would ensure that all relevant associations/ NGOs 
etc. are taken into confidence by the Expert Panel? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) The 
terms of reference of the Expert Panel set up to review the Information 
Technology Act, 2000 are given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
The main objective of the IT Act, 2000 is to promote Electronic Commerce and 
Electronic Governance through the enabling legislation to legally recognise 
the electronic media as equivalent of paper based system including cyber 
security, data protection and cyber crimes. 
Electronic Commerce and Electronic Govemnance are on-going evolution and as 
a result of fast developments, there is need to continuously 
88 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
harmonise the entire infrastructure and statutes with the changing 
requirements. 
The IT Act 2000 is based on the Model Law prepared by United Nation's 
Commission on International Trade and Laws (UNCITRAL) of January 1997. 
However, for reasons explained above, UNCITRAL came up with revised Model 
Law in December 2001. Further the September 11 episode of the World Trade 
Center New York posed certain challeng es for the cyber security and a re-
look was felt essential. In additional there are several other technological 
developments taken place due to convergence of computers, communications 
and content and it is therefore necessary to examine their impact on the 
legislation, if any. 
Therefore, Department of Information Technology has set up the Expert Panel 
to re-examine the Information Technology Act, 2000 in the light of the above 
issues. 
(b) The IT Act 2000 is based on the Model Law prepared by United 
Nation's Commission on International Trade and Laws (UNCITRAL) of 
January 1997. Therefore, the Act had taken tino accont all the relevant 
issues including the international inputs at that point in time.

2531. SHRI DATTAMEGHE: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI RAO 
INDERJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. President Bush signed the "Intelligence Reform and 
Terrorism Preventbn Act of 2004" on December 17,2004. Section 7103 of the Act provides the 
legislative basis for a long-term U.S. policy to Pakistan. It conveys U.S. concerns in

including maintenance of present levels of aid.

aid, covering FY 2005 and FY 2006. 
* An internal reform thrust in Pakistan, focusing on its educational system and 
governance process, particularly in regard to tribal areas. 
* Addressing Pakistani concerns, including outstanding difficulties with its 
neighbours and other countries in the region. 
(c) Government of India understands U.S. efforts in addressing the socio-economic, 
proliferation and terrorism-linked concerns emanating from Pakistan. Government's

2559. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of OCEAN

(COMAPS) has been launched by Government for conduct of studies in the

(c) the benefits, if any, derived by studies carried out; and 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
(d) the details of fund allocated/expe nses incurred on the COMAPS since 
its launching, year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes Sir, the Coastal Ocean 
Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) was launched during the year 
1991-92 to collect data on the levels of Marine Pollutants in the Coastal 
waters of the country. 
(b) The main objective of the progr amme is to analyse the trend of 
decrease/increase of pollutants in the coasal waters of major cities, towns and 
other locations of industrial importance. Collection of data on 25 pollution 
and other related parameters (such as Biochemical Oxygen Demand, 
pathogenic bacteria, toxic metals like cadmium, mercury and lead in 
sediments) at 72-80 locations was carried out with the help of the following 
institutions; 
(i) National Institute of Oceanography, Goa and its Regional Centres at Kochi, 
Mumbai and Visakhapatnam 
(ii) Regional Centre, Central Electro Chemical Research Institute, Chennai 
and Tuticorin/Annamalai University 
(iii) Regional Research Laboratory, Bhubaneswar 
(iv) Centre for Earth Science Studies, Thiruvananthapuram and Zonal Office, 
Central Pollution Control Board, Kolkata 
(v) Andaman and Nicobar Centre for Ocean Science & Technology, 
National Institute of Ocean Technology, Port Blair 
• The Annamalai University/Anna Un iversity and DOD's Integrated 
Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) Project Directorate have 
been entrusted with the task of monitoring of pesticides like Dichloro-
diphenyl-trichloroethane(DDT), Hexachloro-cyclo-hexane (HCH) and 
Endosulfan in edible fish and bivalves. 
• The Regional Research Laboratory, Thiruvananthapuram was entrusted 
with the responsibility of cunducting inter calibration exercises to 
confirm the data quality 
• The task on development of GIS database has been entrusted to (I) 
132 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Institute for Ocean Management, Anna University (ii) ICMAM Project Directorate of 
the Department of Ocean Development 
• The National Institute of Ocean Technology has been entrusted with 
the task of modelling studies to understand the diffusion and 
dispersion characteristics of pollutants. 
(c) As a result of the systematic monitoring of the coastal areas, health of our seas 
could be assessed and areas of low medium and high concentrations of pollutants 
could be identified. The areas of high concentration of pollutants are being monitored 
intensively. Details of these locations are: 
• Areas of clean sea water quality: 
The sea approx. beyond 1 km. along the coastline of India except off Bombay is clean 
and conforms to quality of clean water. In Bombay' the sea off 5 km is clean. This is 
primarily due to the fact that the levels of dissolved oxygen-and other parameters fulfill 
the requirements of clean sea water. 
• Areas of no concern: 
In Vadinar and Kandla of Gujarat, Ratnagiri in Maharashtra, Mandovi and Zuari in 
Goa, Mangalore Port in Karnataka, Cannanore and Calicut in Kerala, Cuddalore in Tamil 
Nadu and the West Bengal Coast, the concentrations of dissolved oxygen was fairly good 
and other toxic elements like ammoma, heavy metals in sediments and biota were slightly 
higher (about 15%) than the clean waters. 
• Areas that need intensive monitoring: 
In Porbondar, Bamanganga estuary, and Vapi industrial estate in Gujarat, 
Mangalore coast in Karnataka, Kochi backwaters, Quilon, Paravur in Kerala and Tuticorin 
and Arumuganeri in Tamil Nadu, Puri in Orissa the levels of dissolved oxygen were 
moderate to normal and however some of the elements like ammonia, pathogenic 
bacteria in sea water and heavy metals in sediments showed higher concentration (about 
25%) then the normal values. Due to the definite source of pollutants chances of increase 
in concentration are likely to be high, these areas need intensive monitoring. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
Areas on concern: 
In Veraval Port in Gujarat, Versova Creek, Mahim Bay and Thane Creek in 
Maharashtra, Veli in Kerala, Visakha patnam Harbout and Kakinada Bay 
(canal) in Andhra Pradesh, the concentrations of dissolved oxygen were nil to 
low during low tide period and improved their levels only moderately (30-
50%) during the high tide period. Further, the levels of toxic metals like 
cadmium and level were high in sediments in some locations (like Thane 
Creek) and pH was very low (Veli). If no control measures are exercised now, 
the areas will become regions of high c oncentrations of pollution in another 5 
to 6 years. 
Levels of organochlorine pesticides like HCH and DDT were analysed in 32 
species of marine fish collected at various locations along the east coast of India. 
The levels of both the chemicals were very much lower than those observed in the 
terrestrial animals and other food items. These levels are well below the limits (5 
parts/billion is the safety limit) set by the Health authorities. This would 
indicate that the marine fish is not contaminated with the pesticide residues in 
the locations from which the samples were collected.

Number of SC/ST families below poverty line 
†2578. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of families related to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

Tribes/Other Backward Classes and weaker section of society living below poverty 
line, State-wise; 
(b) whether the number of such families have increased during the last three

(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of the steps being take n for upliftment of these weaker 
families? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Planning Commission does not estimate the number 
of families living below the Poverty Line in the country. However, it estimates 
poverty at national and state level from the large sample survey on Household 
Consumer Expenditure conducted by the National Sample Organisation (NSSO) 
at an interval of approximately five years. The latest such survey was conducted in 
1999-2000 (NSS 55th Round). On the basis of this Household Consumer 
Expenditure Survey, the percentage of SC/ ST persons living Below Poverty Line 
in 1999-2000 for the major states in enclosed as Statement (See below). The 
corresponding data for Other Backward Classes and weaker sections of 
society are separately not available. 
(b) and (c) The most recent NSSO  data on House hold Consumption 
Expenditure is available only for 1999-2000. As such the data for the last three 
years are not available. 
(d) The Government has taken three pronged strategy of Social 
Empowerment, Economic Empowerment and Social Justice, with an ultimate 
aim to fulfil the Constitutional commitment of raising the status of the Scheduled 
Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes at par with the rest of the 
society. The approach adopted to empower these groups is to achieve overall 
improvement in their socio-economic status through attending to their special 
problems and needs. 
Economic empowerment of these weaker sections of SCs/OBCs and 
Minorities has always been accorded priority especia lly focusing poverty 
alleviation through promoting employment and income generating activities. To this 
effect, various employment-cum-income generation activities are being 
implemented with the objective of making these disadvantaged groups economically 
independent and self-reliant. Towards promoting economic 
154 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
development amongst SCs and STs, Special Central Assistances (SCA) to Special 
Component Plan (SCP) and Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) are being extended to states/UTs on 
the basis of their popultion and relative backwardness. Special efforts are also being 
made through National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation 
(NSCFDC), State SC Development Corporations (SCDCs), National Safai Karamchari 
Finance & Development Corporation (NSKFDC), National Scheduled Tribes Finance & 
Development Corporation (NSTFDC), National Backward Classes Finance and Development 
Corporation (NBCFDC) and National Minorities Development and Finance Corporation 
(NMDFC) for economic development of these socially disadvantaged groups. These 
Corporations also provide skill and entrepreneurial training to unemployed youth through 
reputed training institutions. 
Besides, for poverty alleviation in rural areas, the Ministry of Rural Development is 
implementing two programmes i.e. Sampobrna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) and 
Swamjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) a wage employment and self-employment 
programmes respectively. By these two programmes SC/ST families are also benefited. 
During 2003-04, at national level 8560.24 lakh mandays of employment were generated, of 
which 2827.23 lakh mandays were generated for scheduled castes and 2025.03 lakh mandays 
were generated for scheduled tribes respectively, under self-employment programme, SGSY, 
during 2003-04 the total number of Swarozgaris assisted at national level was 896424 of which 
275186 no. of Swarozgaris were from scheduled castes communities and 13821 no. of 
Swarozgaris were from scheduled tribes communities. 
In urban areas, the Ministry of Urban Employments Poverty Alleviation is implementing 
a Centrally Sponsored urban poverty alleviation programme called Swarna Jayanti Shahari 
Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) through all the States/UTs w.e.f. 1.12.1997. Under the 
Urban, Self-Employment Programme (USEP) component of this scheme urban unemployed 
or underemployed poor living below the poverty line are encouraged to set up self-
employment ventures relating to servicing, petty business and manufacturing 
units. There are no minimum educational qualifications for the beneficiaries under this 
scheme. However, scheme is not applicable to the beneficiaries educated beyond the IX 
standard. There is a special sub-component under USEP component of SJSRY called 
Development of Women and Child in Urban Areas (DWCUA), which is intended for urban 
155

Government of India is generally guided by the recommendations of the Finance

Governments for a fesh period of 20 years at 7.5% rate of interest of States which adopt

all conditions of the scheme.

Launch of Cartosat-I 
2585. DR. K. KASTURIRANGAN: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the planned launch of Cartosat-I this year will provide Survey of 
India with unique inputs to improve mapping methodology; 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the preparatory work to us e the capabilities of Cartosat-I are 
progressing as per plans; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes Sir, Cartosat-I Satellite 
mission, to be launched in the near future has the capability to systematically cover the 
country with along-track stereo images with 2.5m. spatial resolution and 30 Km. swath. 
This unique high-resolution along-track stereo imaging capability, carried out for the first 
time anywhere in the world, will enable operational generation of the Digital Elevation 
Models (DEMs) and various derived value added products thereon. The mission is 
expected to provide enhanced inputs for various large scale mapping applications and 
stimulate newer applications in the urban and rural development; land and water 
resources management; disaster assessment; relief planning and management 
environment impact assessment; and various other applications of Geographical 
Information System. Survey of India could make use of the Cartosat-I data for updating their 
topographic maps, besides making use of them in the generation of Large Scale 
topographic maps. 
(c) and (d) Pilot activities for the generation of along-track stereo images and the Digital 
Elevation Models (DEM) have been satisfactorily completed. Activities pertaining to large scale 
base maps at 1:10,000 scale and related techniques for parameter retrieval etc. are already 
initiated, and these activities are likely to get a further boost after the launch of CartosatI.

High Security Registration Plates 
2602. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will th e Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to make High Security Registration Plates 
mandatory for all vehicles in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the cost involved in replacement of the old 
plates for each vehicles, and rational behind this decision; 
(c) whether Government have fixed any time frame for the replacement of the 
old plates by the new High Security Registration Plates; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIYAPPA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The date of implementation of High Security Registration Plates in 
respect of new vehicles has been prescribed as 31st May, 2005 or any earlier 
date as may be specified by a State Government for that State. 
The main features of the Plates are as under: — 
i. Chromium hologram which is not easily replicable. 
ii. A Retro-reflective film, bearing a verification inscription 'India' at 45 
degree inclination, which cannot be easily replicated. 
iii. Laser Numbering, which is unique in nature containing alpha-numeric 
identification of both Testing Agencies and the manufacturers. 
iv. The registration numbers to be embossed on the plates making it 
difficult to be replicated. 
v. In case of rear registration plate, same is to be fitted with a non-reusable 
snap lock to make it tamper proof. 
183

vi. A Chromium based third registration plate in form of sticker is to be * attached to the 
wind shield, wherein the number of engine and chassis are indicated alongwith the name 
of registering authority. If tampered with, it self destructs. 
vii. In front and rear registration plates, letter IND in blue colour is hot stamped. 
viii. Letters 'IND' in blue colour on extreme left centre of the plate. 
The objective underlying the scheme is to enhance safety of vehicles on the roads 
through improved visibility as also improved the security of vehicles by introducing a 
number of security features in Registration Plates, which would make removal, tampering 
or counterfeiting of such plates difficult. 
The cost of the Plates would be known only after the selection of vendors by the States is 
completed.

Modernising of office of DG-Shipping 
2614. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any effort is being made to modernise the office of the Director 
General of Shipping; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the same systems are in place as fifty years ago; 
(c) whether Government have done any study on how to convert the office of DG 
(Shipping) from a purely regulatory body into one which is also development-
oriented; 
(d) the steps that would be taken to open up the office and simplify the rules and 
procedures; and 
(e) the details of steps proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI 
T.R. BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) No, Sir. The office of Director General of Shipping has undergone change to keep 
pace with the development in maritime sector. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) and (e) the following steps have been taken to open up office of DG (Shipping) and 
relax/simplify the rules and procedures:— 
(i) Relaxation in provisions of 407(1) of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 allowing 
movement of containers by foreign ships between Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (NJPT), 
Mumbai to any other port in India or vice-versa and development of cruise shipping 
industry in India; 
(ii) 50% fee concession and age relaxation allowed for women in maritime training; 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
(iii) more than 125 maritime Training Institutes opened in private sector in 
different parts of the country; 
(iv) continuous up-dation of Maritime Laws to keep pacewith requirements of the 
International Conventions and our shipping industry; 
(v) Tonnage-tax regime has been introduced with effect from 01.01.2005 which 
has resulted in increase in Indian tonnage; 
(vi) Computerization of the Directorate and its allied offices; 
(vii) Indian Database of Seafarers (INDoS) has been set up at the Lal 
Bahadur Shastri College of Advanced martitime Studies and Research, 
with a view to cater to the verification of certificates and documents 
possessed by seafarers; 
(viii) The examination centres at Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai have been 
modernised to ensure that all training and certification is carried out under 
a quality system duly certified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) 
(ix) An additional examination centre at NOIDA near New Delhi, has been 
opened to accommodate the seafarers from the northern parts of the 
country; 
(x) All important Acts, rules orders and circulars issued by DG(S) are 
available on its web site. 
Production of traditional items by MNCs 
2615. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that MNCs have also ventured into manufacturing things 
that have been traditionally undertaken by small scale industries; 
(b) If so, whether Government have ascertained the extent to which the small 
scale industries suffer due to this competition from MNCs; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to provide competitive edge to SSI units? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) As per the notification issued by the Central Government in 
204 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
December 1997, in exercise of the powers conferre d under the Industries 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 industries which are not small scale 
industries (SSIs), including MNCs, can manufacture items reserved for exclusive 
manufacture by the SSI on the condition that 50 per cent of their production 
would be exported. 
(b) No specific study has been conducted to ascertain the extent to which 
the small scale industries might have been affected due to competition from 
MNCs. However, from the fact that the annual rate of growth of production of 
the SSI sector has so far been consistently higher than that of the country's 
industrial sector as a whole, it can be inferred that the SSI sector has generally 
been able to face up to the competition in the market, including that from the 
MNCs. 
(c) To enhance the competitiveness of the SSI units, the Government have 
put in place a slow of measures, whic h include assistance for technological 
upgradation, accessing markets, improved infrastructure, better availability of 
credit, facilities for training and capacity building of entrepreneurs,etc.

2616. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of SMALL    •

country? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) As per the latest information available with the Government based 
on the Third All India Census of the Small Scale Industries with reference to 
the year 2001-02, 8,87,427 registered units were found closed. 
(b) Apart from voluntary closure of SSI units, the main reasons of closure are 
inadequacy/shortage of working capital, fall in demand, changes in 
technology, shortage of raw materials, marketing problems, increase in 
competition, management inadequacies, etc.

Demand for allocation of more Central funds to combat aids in 
Tamil Nadu 
SHRI S. ANBALAGAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, a steep increase in HIV-positive cases 
continues to cause serious concern in the country. This calls for urgent efforts at the 
national level to eradicate AIDS. An estimate shows that 51 lakh men, women and 
children in the country have been affected with HIV/AIDS, by the end of 2003. The 
States of Nagaland and Tamil Nadu have been categorised as high-prevalence 
States. About 14 other States have been categorised as highly vulnerable States. 
So, I request the Government to pay more attention to HIV infection in the country. The 
National Council of AIDS, headed by the hon. Prime Minister, should make all-out 
efforts to end this m enace. Tamil Nadu being a high prevalence State, the State 
Government of Tamil Nadu has taken several steps to control AIDS. The Union 
Government should render more assistance to the States and provide infrastructural 
facilities to fight the disease. More Government hospitals, particularly, in Tamil Nadu 
should be equipped to provide anti-retroviral treatment to HIV affected persons. 
Assistance should also be rendered by the Union Government for opening more 
community care centres in the State, for the promotion of community home-based 
care for HIV positive persons. I have come to know that the Naitonal AIDS 
Research Institute in Pune has developed a vaccine to prevent AIDS. I urge upon the 
Government to expedite human clinical trials of the vaccine. I also urge the 
Government to make continuous research till an effective vaccine is invented to 
prevent AIDS. 
SHRI N.R. GOVINDRAJAR (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I associated myself with the 
Special Mention made by the hon. Member. 
Demand for solar-power fencing in agricultural lands to protect the crops 
from the wild animals 
SHRI N.R. GOVINDRAJAR (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to bring to the notice of the 
august House and to the Government the hardships being faced by the farmers of 
Tamil Nadu, particularly in the areas of Gobichettipalayam constituency, that is 
Sathyamangalam, Anthiyur and Ammapettai to which I belong. There is no doubt 
that economic development counts for the development of a nation; however, 
agricultural development is the foremost for the development of any nation. The 
hardships the farmer faces in bringing up his crops are countless. He has to wait for 
the monsoon, took for loans from the Government and private institution, work in 
field along with his 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
whole family. There is a saying in Tamil which means "breaking the pot while 
churning for the butter". Similarly while waiting for the harvest, the farmers in 
these areas face the threat of wild animals like elephants and boars damaging the 
crops in the night, and thereby resulting in great loss to the farmers and affecting the 
farmers' whole family. I, therefore, urge the Government to come out with a scheme 
with subsidy for solar-power fencing through Non-Conventional Energy Resources as 
in the case of subsidy for agricultural inputs and streetlights through non-conventional 
energy resources. I am sure such schemes would definitely help the farmers to 
establish solar-power fences in their agricultural lands to protect their crops from 
the wild animals as well as to save their lives. Thank you.

Demand to bring a suitable legislation to safeguard the right to 
gender equality 
SHRIMAT IS.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, it is necessary to enact suitable 
legislation to safeguard, preserve and enforcement of the right to gender equality 
of the working women. It has been reported that in so many incidents, female sections 
have been sexually harassed by higher, senior male officials as a tradeoff for declaring 
them fit for commissiong as officers and promotion. Not only for promotion, there are so 
many reasons where the female sections are suffering in so many ways, which cannot 
be expressed. It is the duty of the employer to safeguard the female employee and 
he is the responsible person to take steps for the prosecution of the accused and to 
take preventive steps. He has to take disciplinary action and to form the 
compliance committee headed by a woman and not less than half of its members 
should be women which is helpful for the affected women to initiate complaints and 
get remedy. There is no specific law in this regard. So, I appeal to the 
Government to take suitable measures  including legislation to ensure the 
protection of the working women in all sector. Thank you. 
Need to set up a National Judicial Commission 
SHRI VI JAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): I would like to draw the attention of this 
House to the urgent matter of public importance on setting up a National 
Judicial Commission. 
Sir, legal fraternity and enlightened public have been asking for setting up of a 
National Commission for making appointment of High Court Judges 
236 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
determining their service conditions, drawing up code of ethics, probity, transfers, etc. There 
has been serious erosion of faith in the judicial system in general public and growing suspicion 
in the integrity of higher judiciary. Presently, the Supreme Court has neither administrative 
control over the High Court Judges, nor the power to enquire into their misbehaviour for 
malpractices or corruption. Article 124 (4) of the Constitution provides for the removal of a 
Judge only on the ground of proved misbehav iour or incapacity. The process of 
impeachment is cumbersome. Thus, introduction of effective alternative measures has become 
inescapable because of the constitutionally-assigned role of Supreme Court/High Court for 
protection of the fundamental rights of the people and ensuring justice to the citizens against 
draconian laws. The Commission, an institution so stregetic and transparent, must be 
manned by persons of proven integrity and unalloyed honesty beyond any external 
influence. One alternative could be that appointment of its Members be done by a 
Committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Minister of Law and Jusitce, the Speaker of 
Lok Sabha and the Leaders of the Opposition in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The panel 
of names for the appointment of Judges out of which Commission would finally appoint new 
Judges should have the approval of a Committee comprising Chief Justice of Supreme Court 
and Chief Justices of two High Courts identified by Chief Justice of India on a yearly 
rotational basis. 
Demand for compensation under Crop Insurance Scheme in 
Tamil Nadu 
SHRIR. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to put forward here the present 
gloomy condition of farmers in Thanjavur, Tiruvarur and Nagapattinam districts, who 
are continuously affected because of loss in agriculture for the last four years. They 
are seeking immediate alternative remedy such as provision of compensation under 
the Crop Insurance Scheme, which I had raised before in this august House. 
According to the present norms, the Insurance Corporation considers harvest for three 
consecutive years to calculate the average threshold yield of the present year for the 
provision of compensation to the affected farmers. But, unfortunately, for the last three years 
continuously, farmers of our area have been suffering continuous loss in agriculture. 
For example, for the last three years, our Tiruvarur District has been declared as drought-
affected district, and for the years 2001-2002, 2002-2003, and 2003-2004, insurance 
was declared as 5 per cent, 52 per cent and 47 per cent respectively, as in the year 2001-
2002, our areas were affected 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [24 March, 2005] 
due to adverse flood and during the next two years, by drought. Now, the insurance 
companies, as they did before, have followed the same method of considering the average 
threshold yield of three earlier years. 2001-2002,2002-2003 and 2003-2004 have been 
calculated to find out the actual percentage of loss occurred in the year 2004-2005. If the 
average yield is calculated for the three previous years which are drought years, the affected 
farmers cannot get the exact compensation. Hence, I request the Government to 
direct the concerned authority to calculate average loss of the present year taking into 
consideration the yield often years as special case instead of three years to save the affected 
farmers.

Demand to ensure quality check of petroleum products 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, petroleum products like petrol and diesel are 
supplied to public through retail outlets owned by the Government and private sector. 
For every consumer product, there is a provision for quality check. For checking the 
quality of milk supplied by the Government, co-operative and other agencies, there is 
lactometer. Even the quality of food served in restaurants is checked by the Health 
Inspectors. Even for woollen garments, there is a woolmark and for golden ornaments, there 
is hallmark. But, in the case of petroleum products, there is no provision for quality 
and quantity checks. 
There is a rampant adulteration of petroleum products like petrol and diesel throughout 
the country and especially in Tamil Nadu. Due to poor quality and adulteration of petrol 
and diesel, the pollution level has increased. Already, there is high level of vehicular 
pollution in major cities and this has increased. Sir, since adulterated petrol and diesel is 
being used, the engines of the vehicles are damaged earlier than their life term. Now-a-days, 
every household has a vehicle, and, therefore, all sections of the society are facing the 
problems. Moreover the health of the general public is also affected due to emissions from 
vehicles using adulterated fuel. 
I urge upon the Central Government to introduce a mechanism to check the quality of petrol 
and diesel supplied to the public through retail outlets. 
238 

[24 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In fact, I demand the Government to introduce legislation to check the quality of fuel just 
as in the case of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Adulteration would prove dangerous 
as fuel is also used by the airlines, railways, etc. I suggest that a meter should be kept in 
every retail outlet whether owned by the Government or a private owner so that the public 
can know the quality of fuel used in their vehicles.

referred to specific cases of allotment of land at Rous Avenue and other places by the

market rates.

SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: At the outset, I would like to place before the hon. House the 
various activities of DDA and the role played by it so far in providing housing and other 
amenities for the people of Delhi. 
The DDA was set up under the Delhi Development Act, 1957 to formulate a plan for Delhi and 
effect its development in a planned manner by way of providing shelter, amenities and 
facilities to the existing population and also to make provisions for the future growth of the 
city. In furtherance of its objectives, DDA has so far acquired 69871.22 acres of land and developed 
the acquired land for residential, commercial, industrial, institutional and other purposes like 
allotment to Government organisations, land for slum colonies, Cooperative societies etc. It 
has also undertaken development of green spaces/parks and sports facilities. 
Shri Narayanasamy as well as Shri Manoj Bhattacharya and Shri Rajiv Shukla mentioned 
about the need for construction of houses by DDA for the poor. Shri Narayanasamy also 
referred to a large number of persons registered with DDA for houses and still waiting for 
allotment. In this connection, I would like to mention that in the housing sector, DDA has, 
since inception, constructed 2.90 lakh dwelling units, out of which 55,000 belong to High 
Income Group category, 64,000 to Middle Income Group category and 1.71 lakhs to Low 
Income Group and Economically Weaker Sections categories. Housing for Low Income 
Group and Economically Weaker Sections, thus, constitute nearly 60 per cent of the 
total units

namely, the New Pattern Registration Scheme-1979, Ambedkar Awas Yojana-
1989 and Janta Housing Scheme, 1996. The DDA expects to liquidate these 
pendency by December, 2005. The other two live schemes pertain to

and economically weaker sections category. Further, more than 23,000 houses are

mention that in the allotment of flats, the DDA reserves 25 per cent of the flats for

In so far as allotment of land is concerned, DDA provides land for 
residential, commercial and institutional purposes covering educational 
institutions, hospitals, community halls and social, cultural and religious 
activities, etc. Commercial land is disposed of through auction. In the 
residential category, land is allotted at pre-determined rates only in the case of 
plots for Rohini registrants, allotment of alternative plots to persons whose lands 
are acquired, who are sponsored by the Government of NCT of Delhi and to 
cooperative group housing societies. Other individual residential plots are disposed 
of through auction. In the case of hospitals, land was earlier allotted at Institutional 
Zonal Variant Rates. Since 2001, plot for hospitals, nursing homes are being 
disposed of through auction. DDA provides land for various institutional purposes 
like schools, colleges and other educational  institutions, social, cultural, and 
religious institutions etc. on allotment basis as per the provisions of the Nazul 
Rules and at institutional, zonal variant rates. So far DDA has allotted about 
3500 plots to various categories of institutions. In addition, DDA allots land to 
Government organsiations/local bodies for the purpose of schools, community 
halls, bus terminals, police stations, mother dairy, electric

sub-stations, water pumping stations, hospitals, Delhi Metro, fire stations etc. Since the year 
1999 DDA has allotted land to 921 institutions, out of which 490 allotments, which 
constitutes nearly 53 per cent, are meant for Government agencies/local bodies, while 
431 allotments have been made to various categories of non-Governmental institutions. Out of 
these, 44 were meant for community halls, 49 for religious institutions, 8 for hospitals, 7 
for clubs, 76 for various social, political, cultural organisations and 284 for educational 
institutions which include nursery schools, primary schools and secondary schools. Allotment 
of land is made by the DDA to institutions under the provisions of Nazul Rules and other 
guidelines in force and after taking into consideration the recommendations of various 
authorities. DDA has been making constant efforts to improve and streamline the 
procedure and system of disposal of land. It has also been switching over to disposal 
of land by way of auction in various categories, where the institutions are being run on 
commercial lines. Apart from hospitals, DDA has also decided to auction the plots meant 
for clubs and professional and technical colleges/institutions to ensure greater 
transparency in the method of disposal. 
Allotment of institutional plots at Zonal Variant Rates is made on the basis of 
sponsorship from the State or the Central Government and on the recommendations of the 
Institutional Land Allotment Committee set up in the DDA. In its meetings held in February, 
2003, the Committee had made recommendations for allotment of land in respect of 286 
societies. There were complaints in respect of some societies. The DDA then got the matter 
investigated through its vigilance wing and referred the matter to the Government of NCT 
of Delhi and the sponsoring authorities. The Government of NCT of Delhi initially withdrew all 
sponsorships. Later on, after enquiry, it found 166 cases fit for consideration. Sir, 19 cases 
are presently under investigation by vigilance wing of the DDA. 
Sir, the CBI had also undertaken suo moto investigation in six cases. Out of 286 cases, 
initially recommended by the Institutional Land Allotment Committee, land has so far been 
allotted by the DDA in 54 cases. Out of these cases, three allotments have subsequently 
been cancelled. Two of these relate to community hall sites given to Sarv Dharam Welfare 
Society and Sanskrit Society which were unauthorisedly used as banquet halls. These 
cases were referred to by Shri Narayanasamy in his speech. The third relates to an 
educational society which failed to make payment on time. The remaining cases are 
under consideration.

SHRI EM. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Sir, therefore, I would like to stress upon the 
first part of the Resolution, which says that the backward and poor areas, regions and the 
States should be given priority in the long-term Action Plan. That is a very important thing. We

utilised for Rajasthan. But we do not think on that line. We think only of water, which is 
available now in the form of rivers. We are diverting that water for drinking purpose. We can 
very well say that the Supreme Court has given an order saying that if there is a dispute 
between Haryana and Punjab over the waters of Yamuna river, and if there is a demand for 
drinking water in Delhi, you have to give priority to the drinking water and not to agriculture. 
What is happening now? The Yamuna river is not having water throughout the year. If 
you look at the river, you find it only as drainage water and not as a river. The beautiful Taj 
Mahal, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, is surrounded by only sands, not the 
Yanuma river. This is happening because, in the name of providing drinking water, we are 
pumping out all the water for our daily chores, the household affairs; we are using that 
water for purposes other than drinking. Therefore, there should be a clear restriction that 
says that drinking wafer should be utilized only in such a form and the other water should 
be used only for the purpose of irrigation. 
If water is used for irrigation, it would provide richness to the soil, richness to the earth and

afforestation could be done and lot of fruit-bearing trees could be raised. We are losing 
this wealth. I am giving the example of my own district, which had a lot of fruit-bearing 
trees, but it could not be properly maintained, because the water available was used for 
drinking purposes and not for irrigation.
